surfaces.part: snow step treads (6 steps, each a 1-row edge line plus 4 rows of tread)

answer.evidence: The column scans at x=8, 16 and 23 show the same 5-row period over rows 5-30. Each period is a 1-row darker blue edge line (rows 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30) followed by 4 rows of near-white tread (rows 6-9, 11-14, 16-19, 21-24, 26-29). The silhouette is a full 32-wide rectangle on every row. The treads are the only surface, and no riser or vertical face taller than the 1-row edge line is drawn. That fits stairs seen from above descending away from the viewer: treads stacked with only edge lines between them. No south face of 3 or more rows exists, so it reads as a top-down slab, which is appropriate for a stair terrain tile.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a pale snow-stair patch built from repeated horizontal tread/riser bands. Each band has a white highlight, light blue-white fill, and a blue-grey shadow lip, giving about 5 lightness steps against roughly 6 in the references. The measured facts support it: 9 visible tones per tile against 3 for grass and 7 for paving, and 0% near-flat coverage. Its dark edge pixels are 0% neutral, so the edges lean blue-grey with the snow rather than being a black sticker line. The weaker points are that the bands repeat uniformly and carry little per-step grain or speckle compared with the shaded cobbles in the paving reference. This reads as simple but not shallow, so I give it a marginal pass on the numbers and the visible banding.
